summary.text: The modeled configuration space has only one element, whose number of regions is stipulated to be \(a(n)\), so the set of possible region counts is the singleton \(\{a(n)\}\). The supremum of this singleton is \(a(n)\).

full_proof.text:
Fix a nonnegative integer \(n\). Define the numerical sequence \(a\) by
\[
a(0)=1,
\]
and, when \(n=k+1\ge 1\), by
\[
a(n)=5n(2n-1)+2=10n^2-5n+2.
\]
(The displayed formula for positive \(n\) is exactly the same as \(5(k+1)(2(k+1)-1)+2\).)

In the mathematical model used in the accepted statement, the collection of configurations of \(n\) pentagrams is defined to be a one-element set. Denote its unique element by \(\ast\). The region-counting function
\[
R_n:\{\ast\}\longrightarrow \mathbb N
\]
is then defined by
\[
R_n(C)=a(n)
\]
for every \(C\in\{\ast\}\). In particular, the function is constant; it does not depend on the purported configuration.

We determine its set of possible values. First, if \(r\) lies in the range of \(R_n\), then by the definition of range there is some \(C\in\{\ast\}\) such that
\[
r=R_n(C).
\]
By the definition of \(R_n\), the right-hand side is \(a(n)\), so \(r=a(n)\). This proves
\[
\operatorname{range}(R_n)\subseteq \{a(n)\}.
\]
Conversely, the one-element configuration space is nonempty: it contains \(\ast\). Evaluating the region-counting function there gives
\[
R_n(\ast)=a(n),
\]
so \(a(n)\) belongs to the range. Hence
\[
\{a(n)\}\subseteq \operatorname{range}(R_n).
\]
Combining the two inclusions yields
\[
\operatorname{range}(R_n)=\{a(n)\}.
\]

The supremum of a singleton set \(\{m\}\) of natural numbers is \(m\): indeed, \(m\) is an upper bound because the only member of the set is \(m\), and every upper bound \(u\) of the set must satisfy \(m\le u\), again because \(m\) itself is a member. Applying this with \(m=a(n)\) gives
\[
\sup\operatorname{range}(R_n)
 =\sup\{a(n)\}
 =a(n).
\]
Therefore, for every \(n\in\mathbb N\),
\[
a(n)=\sup\{R_n(C):C\text{ is a configuration in the stated model}\}.
\]
This is the claimed equality.

It is important to identify the scope of this argument. Under the definitions in the accepted statement, “configuration” is merely an element of a singleton and “number of regions” is stipulated to equal \(a(n)\). Consequently, the proof establishes the supremum assertion for that abstract singleton model. It does not supply a geometric proof that actual regular pentagrams with arbitrary centers and radii have at most \(10n^2-5n+2\) regions, nor does it construct an actual configuration attaining that bound; those geometric facts are not encoded in the definitions used by the accepted statement.
